opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing that bureaucracy was the main story. From the inside, the bigger factor was that a lot of the hard work was technical and organizational at the same time.

By early 2023 we had very strong research, but turning it into something you could put in front of hundreds of millions of users is a different problem. You need evaluation, safety review, serving efficiency, multilingual quality, and integration with products that already have huge user bases. At a company of Google's size, each of those has real owners and real standards, and from the outside that can look like bureaucracy. Some of it was legitimate caution, because a mistake at Google's scale has very different consequences than one at a startup.

That said, I think it's fair to say there was friction. Research and product teams weren't always aligned on priorities, and compute was split across many efforts instead of concentrated on one flagship model. When ChatGPT took off, the urgency changed very quickly. People started cutting across team boundaries and making decisions faster. You could see that in how PaLM 2 was positioned and shipped around I/O, and later in the move toward a more unified effort with Gemini.

So my honest take is that the structure slowed some things down, especially coordination. But the deeper lesson was about focus: deciding what the one big bet is and putting the people and compute behind it. Once that clarity existed, things moved a lot faster.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Google’s structure slowed coordination and notes PaLM 2 was shipped around I/O, but does not attribute holding its release until I/O to internal bureaucracy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I can only speak to what I saw from where I sat, and I'd be careful about the word "bureaucracy," because I think it gets used as a catch-all for a lot of different things.

What I'd say is this: by early 2023, Google had a lot of very capable people working on large models, and the technical pieces for something like PaLM 2 were largely there. The question was never really "can we build it." The question was "how do we ship it, to whom, and with what review process." And at a company that size, those are genuinely hard coordination problems, not just paperwork.

So you had research teams who wanted to publish and move fast. You had product teams who had to figure out how a model fits into Search or Workspace without breaking things that billions of people rely on. And you had responsible AI and legal review that, frankly, existed because Google had been burned before. Each of those groups had legitimate reasons for the pace they wanted. The friction came from reconciling them.

Did that slow things relative to what a smaller, more focused organization could do? Honestly, yes, I think it did. OpenAI could put ChatGPT out and iterate in public in a way that Google, culturally and institutionally, was not set up to do at that moment. And once ChatGPT landed in late 2022, you saw the organization reorganize itself pretty quickly around a much tighter deadline. A lot of the "code red" energy was really about collapsing those review loops and getting decisions made in days instead of quarters.

My own view is that the delay was less about any one person saying no and more about there being no single owner who could say yes. When Google consolidated things, with Brain and DeepMind coming together and a clearer product mandate, that's exactly the problem it was trying to fix. Whether PaLM 2 came out a few months later than it could have, I'd say probably. Whether that was purely bureaucracy or also a reasonable amount of caution for a company with that much surface area, I think it's genuinely both.

r001.rationale: The response says internal coordination and review processes probably delayed PaLM 2, but it does not mention holding the release until Google I/O or attribute that specific decision to bureaucracy.

With a model like that, there’s the research work, and then there’s evaluation, safety testing, infrastructure, and coordination with the products that will use it. In a company as large as Google, those dependencies can slow decisions down. But without specific evidence about what held up a particular milestone in early 2023, I wouldn’t say internal bureaucracy was the deciding factor.
